title: Trump Is Gutting America’s Core Geopolitical Advantage
gist: Former USTR and World Bank president Robert Zoellick argues Trump's tariffs and coercion against Canada and Mexico are destroying America's core geopolitical advantage: a secure, integrated continental base. He cites NAFTA-era trade and investment gains, warns that refusing to extend USMCA to 2042 and national-security tariffs are already chilling investment, and urges cooperation on Arctic security, minerals, AI and Mexican rule of law.

insights.claim: China and Russia each must manage 14 neighbors and India six, all dependent on maritime chokepoints, whereas the US borders two benign neighbors and two open oceans.
insights.so_what: North American cohesion underpins the US security premium relative to other major powers.
insights.quote: In contrast, the United States borders two benign neighbors and enjoys open sailing on two vast oceans.
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: Zoellick argues Trump's bullying of Canada and Mexico is destroying a precious geopolitical asset: the strong continental base from which Washington projects power.
insights.so_what: Erosion of North American integration is a structural negative for US strategic and economic position.
insights.quote: The president is destroying a precious geopolitical asset: a strong continental base from which Washington projects power.
insights.locator: A safe, resilient, and adaptive North America
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: North America combines nearly half a billion people with still-growing populations, integrated infrastructure, abundant capital, energy self-sufficiency and capacity to expand oil, gas and renewables output.
insights.so_what: Continental integration is a durable growth and energy-security advantage worth preserving.
insights.locator: The weakening or even breakup of U.S. ties
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: US-Canada trade in goods and services grew from $169 billion in 1988 to about $900 billion in 2024, and US-Mexico trade neared $1 trillion from under $100 billion before NAFTA.
insights.so_what: Shows the scale of trade flows at risk from tariff escalation.
insights.quote: U.S.-Canadian trade in goods and services grew from $169 billion in 1988 to about $900 billion in 2024.
insights.locator: Opponents of NAFTA asserted that Americans
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: US direct investment in Canada rose from $61 billion pre-NAFTA to about $750 billion, Canadian investment in the US from $27 billion to about $500 billion, and US investment in Mexico from $15 billion to $130–150 billion.
insights.so_what: Large cross-border capital stocks are exposed to policy uncertainty.
insights.locator: Cross-border investment has powered this growth
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: The US supplies up to 60 percent of Canada's and about 40 percent of Mexico's imports, while it captures only six to seven cents of each additional dollar China spends on imports.
insights.so_what: Neighbor growth translates far more directly into US exports than growth in distant economies.
insights.quote: When China imports more, for example, the United States receives only six to seven cents of every additional dollar it spends.
insights.locator: Cross-border investment has powered this growth
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: Zoellick contends fears of NAFTA job losses were not borne out: by 2000 US unemployment fell to 3.8 percent, inflation fell, productivity rose and real wages grew, especially for low-wage workers.
insights.so_what: Challenges the populist narrative that underpins current protectionism.
insights.locator: Opponents of NAFTA asserted that Americans
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: Net Mexican immigration to the US fell to zero by 2010 after Mexican-born residents rose from about 760,000 in 1970 to nine million in 2000, which Zoellick links to NAFTA-driven opportunity in Mexico.
insights.so_what: Trade integration can be a migration-management tool; its rollback could reverse that.
insights.quote: But by 2010, Mexican immigration had fallen to net zero
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: USMCA's complex auto rules of origin undermined the sector's global competitiveness and reduced investor protections in Mexico, weakening confidence in the rule of law.
insights.so_what: North American autos face structural competitiveness headwinds from trade rules.
insights.quote: its complex terms to protect regional auto producers undermined that sector’s global competitiveness.
insights.locator: Trump wanted to scrap NAFTA during
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: The Trump administration declined in 2026 to approve extending USMCA to 2042, and the resulting uncertainty is discouraging investment in Canada and Mexico.
insights.so_what: Nearshoring and Canadian/Mexican capex face a policy-uncertainty discount.
insights.quote: uncertainty about its future now discourages investment in Canada and Mexico.
insights.locator: The accord does not expire until 2036
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: In 2025 and 2026 the US imposed high national-security tariffs on Canadian autos, steel, aluminum, iron, metal-intensive equipment, lumber and pharmaceuticals.
insights.so_what: Directly hits integrated North American supply chains in autos, metals, lumber and pharma.
insights.locator: The accord does not expire until 2036
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: Zoellick argues the bigger problem is that the administration wants freedom to ignore the trade agreement whenever it wishes, undermining the rules-based value of USMCA.
insights.so_what: Treaty commitments no longer reliably cap US tariff risk for regional investors.
insights.quote: An even bigger problem is that the Trump administration wants the freedom to ignore the agreement whenever it wishes.
insights.locator: The accord does not expire until 2036
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: Canadians see Trump's tariffs and '51st state' rhetoric as assaults on their economy and independence, while threats of military intervention have revived Mexican fears of US hegemony.
insights.so_what: Political backlash may push neighbors to diversify trade partners away from the US.
insights.locator: The Trump administration’s attack on Canada
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: Zoellick urges US cooperation with Canada on Arctic and maritime security, mineral extraction and trade, and technological innovation, arguing Canada's AI talent and energy resources complement US strengths.
insights.so_what: Points to critical minerals, energy and AI as areas for future US-Canada deals.
insights.quote: Canada’s artificial intelligence talent, research capabilities, and energy resources complement those of the United States
insights.locator: This is an enviable hand to play
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: Zoellick says the US should support Mexico with intelligence and technology to improve security and rule of law, as corruption and criminal enterprises still undermine growth.
insights.so_what: Mexican institutional quality is the key constraint on its nearshoring potential.
insights.locator: Washington also needs to help Mexico
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick

insights.claim: Zoellick predicts the next US president will have an opportunity to change course and restore the continental partnership.
insights.so_what: Policy reversal possible after the current administration, but timing is uncertain.
insights.quote: But the next U.S. president will have an opportunity to change course.
insights.locator: From Seward to Reagan, the Bushes
insights.speaker: Robert B. Zoellick
